source_evidence.observation: Integral conservation is expressed as d/dt ∫ from x₁ to x₂ q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)). Each component of q measures a conserved-quantity density; interval total mass changes only through endpoint fluxes.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; Section 1.1.1, first explanatory paragraph
source_evidence.observation: When the quantity is not conserved, for example because of chemical reactions, the conservation-law model requires source terms.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF pages 26–27; printed pages 4–5; Section 1.1.2
source_evidence.anchor: “provided that q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth” and “does continue to hold”
source_evidence.observation: Deriving the differential equation from integral conservation requires sufficient smoothness. At discontinuities the PDE does not hold classically, while integral conservation remains fundamental and continues to hold. Nonlinear conservation laws can develop discontinuities from smooth initial data.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; Section 1.2, first paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: “cell average of q” and “modified in each time step by the flux through the edges”
source_evidence.observation: Finite volume methods approximate cell integrals or cell averages, with the latter defined as the integral divided by cell volume. Numerical flux functions approximate physical fluxes using approximate cell averages.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; Section 1.2.1
source_evidence.anchor: Equation (1.11) and “q_l = Q_{i−1} and q_r = Q_i”
source_evidence.observation: A Riemann problem combines the hyperbolic equation with piecewise constant initial states separated at x = 0. Neighboring cell averages supply left and right states whose Riemann solution gives information for numerical fluxes and cell-average updates.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 28; printed page 6; Section 1.2.1 continuation
source_evidence.observation: Exact nonlinear Riemann solutions are often too expensive computationally; numerical methods use approximate Riemann solvers.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 28; printed page 6; Section 1.3, first paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: “normal to each edge” and “normal to this plane”
source_evidence.observation: One-dimensional Riemann problems are used in multidimensional finite volume calculations. In two dimensions, edge-normal problems determine flux across polygonal cell edges. In three dimensions, a cell face can be approximated by a plane and a plane-normal Riemann problem used to compute flux.

contract_plain_english: For a rectangular or logically rectangular finite volume grid, LeVeque describes dimensional splitting as the simplest extension of one-dimensional high-resolution methods to more dimensions: solve one-dimensional problems along each coordinate direction in turn using a fractional-step approach. The source says this is often effective in practice, without giving an algorithmic formula or quantitative guarantee in this passage (raw PDF p.28, printed p.6, §1.3, second paragraph). The inherited setting uses integral conservation, approximate cell averages, and numerical fluxes; Riemann problems provide flux information, including through approximate solvers, and integral conservation remains applicable to discontinuous solutions (raw PDF pp.26–28, printed pp.4–6, §§1.1.1–1.2.1). The preceding edge- and face-normal Riemann construction supplies geometric context, but does not specify the details of coordinate splitting (raw PDF p.28, printed p.6, §1.3, first paragraph).
